# Summary {.unnumbered}

This book documents everything built in **canes-cfb-analytics** so far: the data, the
features, the models, how they were evaluated, what worked, what didn't, and the
mistakes that were caught and corrected along the way. It's written to be read top to
bottom by someone who wasn't there, including future me.

## What the project does

It predicts FBS college football games (winner, spread, total, team totals, plus halves
and quarters) and asks one question of every model: **does it know something the
betting market doesn't?** Accuracy alone isn't enough. A model can be accurate and
still lose money if the market is more accurate.

The core model predicts **points per team**. Spread (the difference), total (the sum)
and winner (who scores more) all derive from the two predictions for a game.

## Key results (as of 2026-09-23, 2026 season week 4)

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Enough data? | Yes. 10,630 games (2015–2026), 16,642 FBS-vs-FBS team-game rows for 2015–2025, points by quarter for every game. |
| Best single feature | **Opponent-adjusted ratings** (ridge regression refit every week): error falls from 11.1 to 9.44 points per team. |
| Best model | Tuned random forest on the ratings' residual, plus preseason information (transfer portal, recruiting, new coach, preseason AP poll). |
| How often it's right (2021–2025, unseen seasons) | Winner **70.8%** (books 71.9%), AUC **0.773** (0.793). Against the opening line: spread **50.6%**, total **50.7%**; break-even is 52.4%. Moneyline where it disagrees with the books: **−4.5% ROI** (@sec-reportcard). |
| Versus the market | The books are more accurate by about 0.4–0.6 points on margins and totals. The gap is largest early in the season, in bowls and in blowouts. |
| Interactions? | Small. The signal lives in one-variable curves and thresholds (regression to the mean, talent-gap tails, a returning-production threshold), not in crosses. |
| Betting edge | Not proven. Two pre-registered rules are paper-traded in 2026: **A** (bet the model's side when its total differs from the opener by ≥ 4) and **B** (bet the under when the ratings expect a shootout, which went 55–60% under in every season 2021–2025). |
| A dedicated totals model? | Tried (issue #10). The nonlinear features overfit; the one-line shootout rule held, so the model wasn't adopted. |
| Improving it | Preseason features adopted (early-season gap down ~15%). Ensembles, dedicated models and extra recency weighting were tested under a pre-registered rule and **not** adopted (@sec-improvements). |
| What you use every week | A website with Best Bets, every game, a "Your Call" hunch tool and Betting 101 (@sec-website). |
| Real money? | **No.** A full season of paper results first. |

## How to read this book

- **Foundations** covers the repository, the data and what the data looks like.
- **Features and models** covers feature engineering, the search for nonlinearities, the
  model zoo, tuning, the one-shot test, and halves and quarters.
- **How good is it?** is the report card and the rules used to improve the model without
  fooling ourselves.
- **Betting** covers how predictions become bets, the weekly card website, the decision
  log (including corrections), and what's next.
- The appendices explain how to reproduce everything and define the jargon.

Every number in a table or figure comes from code run against the data, not typed in by
hand, except where a chapter says a table is copied from an experiment log (the slow
experiments: tuning and cross-validated ablations).
